subject: Computing

unit.unitOverview:
The big idea is joyful and simple: we can be artists by giving directions. An artist draws a picture. It is just like telling a friend, “go right, now down, now left, now up,” until a shape appears. This is the very first taste of how computers and drawing robots make pictures.

First, they give and follow directions — the four arrows up, down, left and right. They play the arrows with their whole bodies, follow arrows across a floor grid to reach a friend, and put the steps in the right order. Second, they give instructions for a simple task — a short list of steps (an algorithm) that draws a shape or walks a character along a path.
learningPath: Preview the goals, key words and the tools you will use
Read the concept explainers and study the code examples
Follow the methods and worked examples
Build the activities, debug your work and play the games
Apply, explain and finish the Unit Project and Challenge

provenance.transformation: Structured from the Cambridge Primary Computing 0672 — Stage 1 Teacher & Parent Guide, Activity Sheet and Mini-Project. Teacher-directed prose was rewritten into learner-facing explainers so the unit teaches with no adult present.

outcomes: Name and show the four directions with arrows: up, down, left and right.
Follow a short list of arrow steps to move along a path and reach a target (for example, help Maya reach the garden).
Give simple directions to move something from one square to another.
Understand that a short list of steps in the right order is an algorithm (a list of instructions), and that it needs a start and a stop.
Put a few direction steps into the right order to match a path.
Draw a shape — a square or a rectangle — by following a list of direction steps (be an artist!).
In ScratchJr, add a character and join Move blocks so it walks to a target, then tap the green flag to run it.
Find and fix a wrong step in a short set of directions, and keep trying cheerfully.

toolkit.name: ScratchJr
steps: Open ScratchJr on a tablet.
Tap the house, then tap the plus to start a new project.
Drag the coloured picture blocks together to make your character move.
Tap the green flag to run it.
toolkit.note: Made for ages 5-7. No reading needed and no account to create.

concepts.title: The four directions (unplugged)
concepts.explanation:
A direction is which way something moves. There are four directions we use: up, down, left and right. We show each one with an arrow. Point up! Now down! Now left! Now right!

Try it: You look at each arrow, points the same way with their arm, and traces the arrow with a finger or pencil. Do the first arrow together, then you can finish.

Check yourself: Can you look at an arrow and show the matching direction with your arm? Can you point up, down, left and right on request?
concepts.example: You are giving me directions, and I follow them! Now play a tiny round of Be the Robot: you are the robot, and you give you one arrow at a time — a Right arrow, you step right; an Up arrow, you step forward.
concepts.checkYourself: Can you look at an arrow and show the matching direction with your arm? Can you point up, down, left and right on request?

concepts.title: Follow a path (unplugged)
concepts.explanation:
If we follow a list of direction steps in the right order, we can travel from one place to another. A short list of steps like this is called an algorithm — it just means “a list of instructions.” A good algorithm has a start and a stop.

Lay out your floor grid (three by three squares). Let us give Maya directions to walk to the garden.
concepts.example: One step at a time. Put a toy or a paper Maya on one corner, and a paper garden (a flower) on the far corner.
concepts.checkYourself: Can you see that the steps must be in the right order? Can you point to the start step and the stop step? Can you follow a short list of arrows to reach a target?

concepts.title: Be an artist: draw a shape (unplugged)
concepts.explanation:
Here is the heart of the unit. We can draw a shape by following direction steps with our pencil!

Try it: Give you squared or dotted paper.

Check yourself: Can you see that a shape can be made by following a list of directions? Can you point to a square and a rectangle in the room? Can you follow the steps to draw a closed square?
concepts.example: If we move our pencil right, then down, then left, then up, we draw a square. We are being artists, using directions.
concepts.checkYourself: Can you see that a shape can be made by following a list of directions? Can you point to a square and a rectangle in the room? Can you follow the steps to draw a closed square?

concepts.title: Directions in ScratchJr
concepts.explanation:
Now we give directions on the tablet. In ScratchJr, the blue Move blocks are our four arrows. We join them to make a character walk to a target, then tap the green flag to run our program.

The yellow block starts things. The blue arrow blocks are our directions.
concepts.example: Show ScratchJr on a big screen so everyone can see. Open a new project, choose a garden Background, add a bee, and add a flower for it to reach.
concepts.checkYourself: Can you drag and join two or three Move blocks in an order that reaches the flower, and run it with the green flag? Can you point to a block and say which direction it moves? Can you add a character?

concepts.title: Be an artist: the Mini-Project
concepts.explanation:
You draw a square window by following direction steps, then you find and fix a wrong step in another set of directions. This session and the Mini-Project sheet go hand in hand.

We are going to draw a window for our classroom by following directions. Show the dotted square on the Mini-Project sheet.
concepts.example: Do it yourself: be an artist: the Mini-Project. Work through it slowly, then check what you did against the explanation above.
concepts.checkYourself: Did you find and fix the wrong step? Did you keep trying with a smile? Does you follow the steps to draw a closed square?

debugging.cause: A common misunderstanding about this idea.
debugging.fix: It matters a lot. Right-then-up reaches the garden; up-then-right may not. Muddle the steps on purpose and you can see the character go the wrong way.

debugging.symptom: An arrow points wherever I look.
debugging.cause: A common misunderstanding about this idea.
debugging.fix: An arrow always points the same way on the page — up, down, left or right — and does not change when we turn our heads.

debugging.symptom: I need a different step for every side.
debugging.cause: A common misunderstanding about this idea.
debugging.fix: We use the same four little moves — right, down, left, up. Drawing a shape is just a few simple steps in order.

debugging.symptom: A square and a rectangle are the same.
debugging.cause: A common misunderstanding about this idea.
debugging.fix: Both have four sides and four corners, but a square's sides are all equal, and a rectangle has two long sides and two short sides.

esafety.title: Check before you trust
esafety.text: Anyone can put anything on the internet, so not everything you read is true. Check an important fact on a second, different website, and ask an adult you trust if you are not sure.

esafety.title: Tell someone if something worries you
esafety.text: If anything online upsets you, or someone asks you for personal information or to keep a secret, stop, leave the page and tell an adult you trust straight away. It is never your fault.

esafety.title: Respect other people's work
esafety.text: Pictures, music and writing belong to whoever made them. Use work that is free to use, and say where you got it. Your own work belongs to you — put your name on it.

selfAssessment: I can name and show the four directions with arrows: up, down, left and right.
I can follow a short list of arrow steps to move along a path and reach a target (for example, help Maya reach the garden).
I can give simple directions to move something from one square to another.
I can understand that a short list of steps in the right order is an algorithm (a list of instructions), and that it needs a start and a stop.
I can put a few direction steps into the right order to match a path.
I can draw a shape — a square or a rectangle — by following a list of direction steps (be an artist!).
I can in ScratchJr, add a character and join Move blocks so it walks to a target, then tap the green flag to run it.
I can find and fix a wrong step in a short set of directions, and keep trying cheerfully.
